53

We regularly assess our ability to realize our deferred tax assets on a quarterly basis and will establish a valuation allowance if it is more-likely-than-not that some portion of the deferred tax assets will not be realized. As of September 26, 2026, we maintain a valuation allowance on deferred tax assets related to U.S. federal foreign tax credit carryforwards and California research and development credit carryforwards. We also maintain a full valuation allowance on our Canada deferred tax assets, and a partial valuation allowance on our U.K. deferred tax assets. We will continue to assess the need for a valuation allowance against our remaining deferred tax assets and may increase or decrease our valuation allowance materially in the future. Any such change will be recognized as a component of the provision for income taxes in the period in which the change in assessment occurs.
Our provision for income taxes may be impacted by changes in the geographic mix of earnings, acquisitions, changes in the realizability of deferred tax assets, changes in our uncertain tax positions, the results of income tax audits, settlements with tax authorities, the expiration of statutes of limitations, the implementation of tax planning strategies, tax rulings, court decisions, and changes in tax laws and regulations. It is also possible that significant negative or positive evidence may become available that causes us to change our conclusion regarding whether a valuation allowance is needed on certain of our deferred tax assets, which would affect our income tax provision in the period of such change.
We also evaluate changes to regulations and requirements in the international jurisdictions where we conduct our business. For additional information, refer to Part II Item 1A “Risk Factors”.
Financial Condition
Liquidity and Capital Resources
As of September 26, 2026 and June 27, 2026, our cash and cash equivalents were $1,272.2 million and $2,043.5 million, respectively. As of September 26, 2026 and June 27, 2026, our short-term investments of $707.4 million and $694.9 million, respectively, were all held in the United States. Cash equivalents and short-term investments are primarily comprised of money market funds, treasuries, agencies, high quality investment grade fixed income securities, certificates of deposit, and commercial paper. Our investment policy and strategy provide for diversification of investments and is focused on the preservation of capital and supporting our liquidity requirements.
The total amount of cash held by the non-United States entities as of September 26, 2026 and June 27, 2026 was $426.9 million and $417.9 million, respectively, which was primarily held by entities incorporated in the United Kingdom, Japan, Hong Kong, China, Switzerland, and Thailand. Although cash currently held in the United States, as well as cash generated in the United States from future operations, is expected to cover our normal operating requirements, a substantial amount of additional cash could be required for other purposes, such as capital expenditures to support our business and growth, including costs associated with increasing internal and external manufacturing capabilities, strategic transactions and partnerships, and future acquisitions.
Our intent is to indefinitely reinvest funds held outside the United States and, except for the funds held in the Cayman Islands, the British Virgin Islands, and Hong Kong, as well as certain subsidiaries in China and Japan, our current plans do not demonstrate a need to repatriate them to fund our domestic operations. However, if in the future, we encounter a significant need for liquidity domestically or at a particular location that we cannot fulfill through borrowings, equity offerings, or other internal or external sources, or the cost to bring back the money is not significant from a tax perspective, we may determine that cash repatriations are necessary or desirable. Repatriation could result in additional material taxes. These factors may cause us to have an overall tax rate higher than other companies or higher than our tax rates in the past. Additionally, if conditions warrant, we may seek to obtain additional financing through debt or equity sources. To the extent we issue additional shares, it may create dilution to our existing stockholders. However, any such financing may not be available on terms favorable to us or may not be available at all.
Beginning in fiscal year 2023, the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017 requires taxpayers to capitalize research and development expenditures and amortize domestic expenditures over five years and foreign expenditures over fifteen years. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (“OBBBA”) enacted in July 2025 eliminates capitalization of domestic research and development expenditures for taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2025, but retains the requirement to amortize foreign research and development expenditures over 15 years. In addition, the OBBBA permits all taxpayers who paid or incurred domestic research and development expenses in tax years beginning on or after January 1, 2022 and before January 1, 2025 to elect to deduct any remaining unamortized amount over a one-year period or ratably over a two-year period (at the taxpayer’s election), accelerating the benefit of such expenses. We have evaluated these changes and included their impact in our tax provision for fiscal year 2026.
54

Liquidity and Capital Resources Requirements
We believe that our cash and cash equivalents as of September 26, 2026, available borrowing capacity under our Credit Agreement, and cash flows from our operating activities will be sufficient to meet our liquidity and capital spending requirements for at least the next 12 months from the issuance of our financial statements for the first quarter of our fiscal year 2027.
There are a number of factors that could positively or negatively impact our liquidity position, including:
•the settlement of any conversion or redemption of our convertible notes in cash;
•global economic conditions which affect demand for our products and services and impact the financial stability of our suppliers and customers, including the impact of uncertainty in the banking and financial services industries;
•fluctuations in demand for our products as a result of changes in regulations, tariffs or other trade barriers, and trade relations in general;
•changes in accounts receivable, inventory or other operating assets and liabilities, which affect our working capital;
•increase in capital expenditures to support our business and growth, including increases in manufacturing capacity;
•the tendency of customers to delay payments or to negotiate favorable payment terms to manage their own liquidity positions;
•timing of payments to our suppliers;
•volatility in fixed income and credit, which impact the liquidity and valuation of our investment portfolios;
•cost and availability of credit, which may impact available financing for us, our customers or others with whom we do business;
•volatility in foreign exchange markets, which impacts our financial results;
•possible investments or acquisitions of complementary businesses, products or technologies, or other strategic transactions or partnerships;
•issuance of debt or equity securities, or other financing transactions, including bank debt;
•potential funding of pension liabilities either voluntarily or as required by law or regulation; and
•acquisitions or strategic transactions.

Cash Flows
Our balance of cash and cash equivalents decreased by $771.3 million from $2,043.5 million as of June 27, 2026 to $1,272.2 million as of September 26, 2026. The decrease in cash and cash equivalents during the three months ended September 26, 2026 was due to cash used in financing activities of $804.4 million and cash used in investing activities of $234.6 million, offset by cash from operating activities of $267.7 million.
Operating Cash Flow
Cash from operating activities was $267.7 million during the three months ended September 26, 2026, which primarily reflects a net income of $360.3 million and non-cash items of $208.6 million, partially offset by changes in operating assets and liabilities of $301.2 million. Changes in operating assets and liabilities were primarily driven by a $105.4 million increase in accounts receivable mainly driven by higher revenue, a $114.2 million increase in inventories driven by inventory builds to support market demand and a $114.2 million increase in prepayments and other current and non-current assets primarily driven by increase in value-added-tax receivables due to higher capital expenditures and inventory purchases and inventory-related prepayments with certain suppliers, a $78.8 million decrease in income tax liabilities primarily due to income tax payments, and a $13.6 million decrease in accrued payroll and related expenses mainly driven by payments of employee cash bonuses, offset by an $87.0 million increase in accounts payable primarily due to higher inventory purchases and capital expenditures, and a $38.5 million increase in accrued expenses and other current and non-current liabilities driven by contractual liabilities.
Cash from operating activities was $57.9 million during the three months ended September 27, 2025, which primarily reflects a net income of $4.2 million and non-cash items of $108.3 million, offset by changes in operating assets and liabilities of $54.6 million. Changes in operating assets and liabilities were primarily driven by a $28.8 million increase in accounts payable primarily due to higher inventory purchases and capital expenditures, an $11.4 million increase in accrued payroll and related expenses mainly driven by our accrual on employee cash bonuses, outstanding payroll taxes related to stock-based compensation and ESPP contribution, and a $24.8 million increase in accrued expenses and other current and non-current liabilities driven by contractual liabilities, accrued interest on convertible notes and provision for non-cancellable commitments, offset by a $56.9 million increase in accounts receivable mainly driven by higher revenue, and a $57.5 million increase in inventories driven by inventory builds to support market demand.

Cash used in investing activities of $67.8 million during the three months ended September 27, 2025 was attributable to $76.2 million of capital expenditures, offset by $8.4 million of net proceeds from sales or maturities of short-term investments.

ITEM 3. QUANTITATIVE AND QUALITATIVE DISCLOSURES ABOUT MARKET RISK
Foreign Exchange Risk
We conduct our business and sell our products to customers primarily in Asia, Europe, and North America. Due to the impact of changes in foreign currency exchange rates between the U.S. Dollar and foreign currencies, we recorded a net foreign exchange loss of $6.7 million and a net foreign exchange gain of $1.5 million in the condensed consolidated statements of operations for the three months ended September 26, 2026 and September 27, 2025, respectively.
Although we sell primarily in the U.S. Dollar, we have foreign currency exchange risks related to our expenses denominated in currencies other than the U.S. Dollar, principally the Chinese Yuan, Canadian Dollar, Thai Baht, Japanese Yen, Hong Kong Dollar, UK Pound, Swiss Franc, and Euro. The volatility of exchange rates depends on many factors that we cannot forecast with reliable accuracy. In the event our foreign currency denominated monetary assets and liabilities, sales or expenses increase, our operating results may be affected to a greater extent by fluctuations in the exchange rates of the currencies in which we do business as compared with the U.S. dollar.
Equity Price Risk
We are exposed to equity price risk related to the conversion options embedded in our 2032 Notes, 2029 Notes, 2028 Notes and 2026 Notes.
We issued the 2032 Notes in September 2025, 2029 Notes in June 2023, the 2028 Notes in March 2022 and the 2026 Notes in December 2019. As of September 26, 2026, the aggregate principal amounts of the 2032 Notes, 2029 Notes, 2028 Notes and 2026 Notes were $1,265.0 million, $27.2 million, $21.1 million, and $4.2 million, respectively, and bear interest at a rate of 0.375%, 1.50%, 0.50% and 0.50% per year, respectively. Since the convertible notes bear interest at fixed rates, we have no financial statement risk associated with changes in market interest rates. However, the potential value of the shares to be distributed to the holders of our convertible notes changes when the market price of our stock fluctuates. The 2032 Notes, 2029 Notes, 2028 Notes and 2026 Notes will mature on March 15, 2032, December 15, 2029, June 15, 2028 and December 15, 2026, respectively, unless earlier repurchased by us or converted pursuant to their terms, at a conversion price of approximately $187.77 per share for the 2032 Notes, $69.54 per share for the 2029 Notes, $131.03 per share for the 2028 Notes and $99.29 per share for the 2026 Notes.
In connection with the issuance of the 2032 Notes, we entered into the 2032 Capped Call Options with the 2032 Capped Call Counterparties. The cap price of the 2032 Capped Call Options was initially $268.24 per share, and is subject to certain adjustments under the terms of the 2032 Capped Call Options. To the extent the market price per share of our common stock, as measured under the terms of the 2032 Capped Call Options, exceeds the cap price of the 2032 Capped Call Options, there would be dilution and/or there would not be an offset of any potential cash payments in excess of the principal amount of converted 2032 Notes, in each case, to the extent that such market price exceeds the cap price of the 2032 Capped Call Options.
Interest Rate Fluctuation Risk
As of September 26, 2026, we had cash, cash equivalents, and short-term investments of $1,979.6 million. Cash equivalents and short-term investments are primarily comprised of money market funds, treasuries, agencies, high quality investment grade fixed income securities, certificates of deposit, and commercial paper. Our investment policy and strategy is focused on the preservation of capital and supporting our liquidity requirements. We do not enter into investments for trading or speculative purposes. As of September 26, 2026, the weighted-average life of our investment portfolio was approximately twelve months.
59

Our fixed-income portfolio is subject to fluctuations in interest rates, which could affect our results of operations. Based on our investment portfolio balance as of September 26, 2026, a hypothetical increase or decrease in interest rates of 1% (100 basis points) would have resulted in a decrease or an increase in the fair value of our portfolio of approximately $7.4 million, and a hypothetical increase or decrease in interest rates of 0.50% (50 basis points) would have resulted in a decrease or an increase in the fair value of our portfolio of approximately $3.7 million.
On December 19, 2025, we entered into a Credit Agreement providing for a senior secured revolving credit facility in an aggregate principal amount of $400.0 million, including a $23.0 million sublimit for the issuance of letters of credit. At our option, borrowings bear interest at a variable rate tied to either a base rate or a term Secured Overnight Financing Rate, plus, in each case, a margin based on our secured net leverage ratio. Consequently, our interest expense could fluctuate due to the variable interest rates applicable to any borrowing under the Credit Agreement. As of September 26, 2026, there were no borrowings outstanding under the Credit Agreement.
Bank Liquidity Risk
As of September 26, 2026, we had approximately $489.2 million of unrestricted cash (excluding cash equivalents) in operating accounts that are held with domestic and international financial institutions. These cash balances could be lost or become inaccessible if the underlying financial institutions fail or if they are unable to meet the liquidity requirements of their depositors and if they are not supported by the national government of the country in which such financial institution is located. Notwithstanding, we have not incurred any losses to date and have had full access to our operating accounts. We believe any failures of domestic and international financial institutions could impact our ability to fund our operations in the short term. The value of our investment portfolio could also be impacted if we hold debt instruments which were issued by any institutions that fail or become illiquid. Our ability to obtain raw materials for our supply chain and collections of cash from sales may be unduly impacted if any of our vendors or customers are affected by illiquidity events.
60

ITEM 4. CONTROLS AND PROCEDURES 
(a) Evaluation of Disclosure Controls and Procedures
Our management is responsible for establishing and maintaining adequate internal control over financial reporting. Management, with the participation of our chief executive officer and our chief financial officer, evaluated the effectiveness of our disclosure controls and procedures as of September 26, 2026. The term “disclosure controls and procedures,” as defined in Rules 13a-15 and 15d-15 under the Exchange Act, means controls and other procedures of a company that are designed to ensure that information required to be disclosed by a company in the reports that it files or submits under the Exchange Act is recorded, processed, summarized and reported within the time periods specified in the SEC’s rules and forms. Disclosure controls and procedures include, without limitation, controls and procedures designed to ensure that information required to be disclosed by a company in the reports that it files or submits under the Exchange Act is accumulated and communicated to our management, including its principal executive and principal financial officers, as appropriate to allow timely decisions regarding required disclosure. Management recognizes that any controls and procedures, no matter how well-designed and operated, can provide only reasonable assurance of achieving their objectives, and management necessarily applies its judgment in evaluating the cost-benefit relationship of possible controls and procedures. Based on the evaluation of our disclosure controls and procedures, as of September 26, 2026, our chief executive officer and chief financial officer concluded that our disclosure controls and procedures were effective at a reasonable assurance level.
(b) Changes in Internal Control over Financial Reporting
There were no changes in our internal control over financial reporting identified in connection with the evaluation required by Exchange Act Rules 13a-15(d) or 15d-15(d) that occurred during the quarter ended September 26, 2026 that have materially affected, or are reasonably likely to materially affect, our internal control over financial reporting.
(c) Inherent Limitations on Effectiveness of Controls
Our management, including the CEO and CFO, recognizes that our disclosure controls and procedures or our internal control over financial reporting cannot prevent or detect all possible instances of errors and all fraud. A control system, no matter how well designed and operated, can provide only reasonable, not absolute, assurance that the control system's objectives will be met. The design of a control system must reflect the fact that there are resource constraints, and the benefits of controls must be considered relative to their costs.

ITEM 1A. RISK FACTORS
Our business, financial condition and results of operations are subject to a number of trends, risks and uncertainties. We review and, where applicable, update our risk factors each quarter. There have been no material changes from the risk factors disclosed in Part I, Item 1A of our Annual Report on Form 10-K for the year ended June 27, 2026, other than the addition of the following risk factors:
Risks Related to Our Business
New or expanded FCC restrictions could adversely affect our business and results of operations.
The Federal Communications Commission (“FCC”) maintains a “Covered List” of communications equipment and services deemed to pose an unacceptable risk to U.S. national security or the safety and security of U.S. persons. FCC rules restrict authorization, importation, marketing and sale of certain listed equipment. The FCC is reportedly considering adding optical transceivers to the Covered List; however, no final rule specifically addressing optical transceivers has been issued. As such, timing and scope of any final rule remains uncertain. If optical transceivers or other Lumentum products are made subject to these or similar restrictions, this could affect our ability to manufacture or source certain products or components outside the United States, including without limitation optical transceivers. These restrictions could limit our ability to obtain or maintain required authorizations or to import, market or sell affected products in the United States. Restrictions affecting products sold by our suppliers or customers could also disrupt our supply chain or reduce demand. We may need to redesign products, qualify alternative components or suppliers, or modify our manufacturing or supply chain, increasing costs, delaying deliveries or reducing margins. These restrictions and related impacts could adversely affect our sales, market share, business, financial condition and results of operations.
Risks Related to the Proposed Merger with Marvell
Because the Exchange Ratio is fixed and the market price of Marvell Common Stock will fluctuate, our stockholders cannot be certain of the value of the merger consideration they will receive.
On November 1, 2026, we entered into a Merger Agreement with Marvell and two of its wholly owned subsidiaries, pursuant to which, upon the terms and subject to the conditions of the Merger Agreement, we will become a wholly owned subsidiary of Marvell. At the Effective Time, each share of our Common Stock issued and outstanding immediately prior to the Effective Time, subject to certain exceptions in the Merger Agreement, will be converted into the right to receive 4.500 shares of Marvell Common Stock (such ratio, the Exchange Ratio), with cash in lieu of fractional shares. Shares of our Series A Convertible Preferred Stock will be converted into the right to receive Marvell Common Stock based on the Exchange Ratio or, if the holder so elects, shares of a new series of Marvell Series B Preferred Stock.
The Exchange Ratio is fixed and will not be adjusted for changes in the market price of Marvell Common Stock or our Common Stock, and the Merger Agreement does not permit either party to terminate the Merger Agreement solely because of changes in the market price of either company’s stock. Accordingly, the market value of the merger consideration will vary from the date of announcement of the Merger, from the date of this Quarterly Report on Form 10-Q, from the date of the joint proxy statement/prospectus relating to the Merger and from the date of our special meeting of stockholders to approve the Merger, and the market value of the Merger consideration at the Effective Time may be higher or lower than its value on any of those dates. Changes in the market price of Marvell Common Stock may result from a variety of factors, many of which are beyond our and Marvell’s control, including changes in Marvell’s business, operations and prospects, market assessments of the likelihood that the Merger will be completed and of the timing of the Merger, regulatory considerations, general market, industry and economic conditions and the other factors described in Marvell’s filings with the SEC. Because the Merger is expected to be completed some time after our special meeting, at the time of the meeting our stockholders will not know the market value of the Marvell Common Stock that they will receive upon completion of the Merger.
63

The Merger is subject to a number of conditions, some of which are outside our control, and the Merger may not be completed on the anticipated timeline or at all.
Completion of the Merger is subject to the satisfaction or, to the extent permitted, waiver of a number of conditions, including, among others: (a) adoption of the Merger Agreement by our stockholders; (b) approval by Marvell’s stockholders of the issuance of Marvell Common Stock in the Merger and of an amendment to Marvell’s certificate of incorporation to increase the number of authorized shares; (c) the expiration or termination of the applicable waiting period under the Hart-Scott-Rodino Antitrust Improvements Act of 1976, as amended, and the receipt of certain other required regulatory approvals; (d) the absence of a legal restraint imposed by certain governmental authorities preventing the completion of the Merger; (e) the effectiveness of the registration statement on Form S-4 to be filed by Marvell in connection with the Merger; (f) authorization for listing on the Nasdaq Global Select Market of the shares of Marvell Common Stock to be issued in the Merger; (g) the accuracy of the representations and warranties of each party (subject to certain qualifications); (h) the performance in all material respects by each party of its obligations under the Merger Agreement; and (i) the absence of a material adverse effect on either us or Marvell. Neither we nor Marvell can control whether the stockholders of either company will approve the Merger-related proposals or whether or when the required regulatory approvals will be obtained.
Governmental authorities may refuse to grant required approvals, may delay their review or may seek to impose conditions on their approval, including requirements to divest assets or businesses, license intellectual property, enter into commercial or behavioral commitments or otherwise restrict the conduct of our or Marvell’s businesses. Marvell is not required under the Merger Agreement to accept certain remedies that would reasonably be expected to be material and adverse to the combined businesses of Marvell and us, taken as a whole, or that are not conditioned on completion of the Merger, and the imposition of any such condition could result in the Merger not being completed. Any such conditions, if accepted, could also reduce the anticipated benefits of the Merger or adversely affect the combined company’s business. In addition, either party may terminate the Merger Agreement if the Merger has not been completed by November 1, 2027, which date may be extended in certain circumstances to February 1, 2028, May 1, 2028 and August 1, 2028 if required regulatory approvals have not been obtained, and in certain other specified circumstances. We cannot assure you that the conditions to the completion of the Merger will be satisfied or waived, that the Merger will be completed on the anticipated timeline or at all, or that the Merger Agreement will not be terminated.

Failure to complete the Merger could negatively affect our business, financial condition, results of operations and the market price of our common stock.
If the Merger is not completed for any reason, our ongoing business may be adversely affected and, without realizing any of the anticipated benefits of the Merger, we would be subject to a number of risks, including the following:
•to the extent that the current market price of our Common Stock reflects an assumption that the Merger will be completed, the market price of our Common Stock could decline significantly;
•we have incurred, and will continue to incur, significant costs, expenses and fees for professional services and other transaction costs in connection with the Merger, a substantial portion of which we must pay whether or not the Merger is completed;
•under certain circumstances, including if the Merger Agreement is terminated because our board of directors changes its recommendation that our stockholders adopt the Merger Agreement or so that we may enter into a definitive agreement providing for a superior proposal, or in certain circumstances following the termination of the Merger Agreement after an alternative acquisition proposal has been made, we may be required to pay Marvell a termination fee of $2.9 billion, which would adversely affect our financial condition and liquidity;
•the disruption to our business resulting from the announcement and pendency of the Merger, including adverse changes in our relationships with customers, suppliers, partners and employees, may continue or intensify;
•we may experience negative reactions from the financial markets, including analysts and investors, and from our customers, suppliers, partners and employees;
•we will have been subject to restrictions on the conduct of our business, and may have forgone business opportunities, during the pendency of the Merger; and
•we could be subject to litigation related to the Merger or to any failure to complete the Merger.
64

In addition, if the Merger is not completed, our board of directors may seek other strategic alternatives, which may not be available on terms as favorable to our stockholders as the Merger, or at all. The occurrence of any of these events, individually or in the aggregate, could have an adverse effect on our business, financial condition, results of operations and the market price of our Common Stock.
Our stockholders will have a significantly reduced ownership and voting interest in, and will exercise less influence over the management of, the combined company.
Upon completion of the Merger, our stockholders will become stockholders of Marvell and will hold a significantly smaller percentage ownership of the combined company than they currently hold of our company. Accordingly, our former stockholders will have less influence over the management and policies of the combined company than they currently have over our management and policies, and only three members of our current board of directors are expected to be appointed to the Marvell board of directors following the Effective Time.
The combined company may be unable to integrate our business successfully and realize the anticipated benefits of the Merger, which could adversely affect the market price of Marvell common stock following the Merger.
The success of the Merger will depend, in part, on the combined company’s ability to realize the anticipated benefits and synergies from combining our business with Marvell’s business. Integrating two large and complex businesses is a difficult, costly and time-consuming process, and the combined company may encounter difficulties, including the loss of key employees, customers, suppliers or other business partners, difficulties in integrating operations, technologies, manufacturing facilities, supply chains and systems, inconsistencies in standards, controls, procedures and policies, unanticipated costs, liabilities or delays, and the diversion of management’s attention. Any regulatory conditions imposed in connection with the Merger could also limit the anticipated benefits. If the combined company is not able to successfully integrate our business with Marvell’s business, or if the anticipated benefits and synergies of the Merger are not realized fully, within the expected timeframe or at all, the market price of Marvell Common Stock, and therefore the value of the Merger consideration received by our stockholders, may decline.
After the Merger, our stockholders will hold Marvell Common Stock, the market price of which may be affected by factors different from those affecting the market price of our Common Stock, and their rights will be governed by Marvell’s organizational documents.
Upon completion of the Merger, holders of our Common Stock will become holders of Marvell Common Stock. Marvell’s business and financial position differ from ours, and the results of operations of the combined company, as well as the market price of Marvell Common Stock, may be affected by factors different from those currently affecting our results of operations and the market price of our Common Stock, including risks relating to Marvell’s business described in Marvell’s filings with the SEC. In addition, the issuance of a substantial number of shares of Marvell Common Stock in the Merger, and sales of those shares in the public market following the Merger, could depress the market price of Marvell Common Stock. Following the Merger, the rights of our former stockholders will be governed by Marvell’s certificate of incorporation, as amended in connection with the Merger, and bylaws, which differ in certain respects from our certificate of incorporation and bylaws.

As a result of the Merger, our current and prospective employees could experience uncertainty about their future with us or the combined company. As a result, key employees may depart because of issues relating to such uncertainty or a desire not to remain with Lumentum following the completion of the Merger.
As a result of the Merger, our current and prospective employees could experience uncertainty about their future with us or the combined company, or decide that they do not want to continue their employment with us or the combined company. As a result, key employees may depart because of issues relating to such uncertainty or a desire not to remain with Lumentum either prior to or following the completion of the Merger. Losses of officers, key employees or other employees could materially harm our business, results of operations and financial condition. Such adverse effects could also be exacerbated by a delay in the completion of the Merger for any reason, including delays associated with obtaining requisite regulatory approvals or the approval of our stockholders. We may also experience challenges in hiring new employees during the pendency of the Merger, or if the Merger Agreement is terminated, which could harm our ability to grow our business, execute on our business plans or enhance our operations. If the Merger is consummated, the combined
65

company may be less attractive to current and prospective employees, which could harm the business and prospects of the combined company.
The Merger Agreement restricts the conduct of our business before the completion of the Merger.
The Merger Agreement requires us, subject to certain exceptions, to conduct our business in the ordinary course prior to the completion of the Merger and restricts us, without Marvell’s consent, from taking certain specified actions until the Merger is completed or the Merger Agreement is terminated. These restrictions may prevent us from pursuing business opportunities or strategies that arise prior to the completion of the Merger, including making acquisitions, investments or capital expenditures, disposing of assets, incurring indebtedness, issuing equity securities or entering into or amending certain material contracts, and may affect our ability to respond effectively to competitive pressures, industry developments and customer demand. If the Merger is not completed, these restrictions may also have placed us at a disadvantage relative to our competitors. These restrictions could adversely affect our business, financial condition and results of operations.
The Merger Agreement contains provisions that could discourage a potential competing acquirer.
The Merger Agreement contains “no-shop” provisions that, subject to limited exceptions, restrict our ability to solicit, initiate or knowingly encourage proposals for alternative transactions from third parties, to participate in discussions or negotiations with, or provide nonpublic information to, third parties in connection with any alternative transaction, or to enter into an agreement providing for an alternative transaction. In addition, our board of directors may change its recommendation that our stockholders adopt the Merger Agreement, and we may terminate the Merger Agreement to enter into a definitive agreement providing for a superior proposal, only in limited circumstances and subject to Marvell’s right to negotiate revisions to the terms of the Merger Agreement, and we may be required to pay Marvell a termination fee of $2.9 billion in certain of those circumstances. These provisions could discourage a third party that might have an interest in acquiring all or a significant part of our company from considering or proposing an alternative transaction, even if that party were prepared to pay consideration with a higher value than the Merger consideration, or could result in a potential acquirer proposing to pay a lower price than it would otherwise have proposed to pay.
Litigation relating to the Merger could prevent or delay the completion of the Merger or otherwise adversely affect our business.
Lawsuits are frequently brought against public companies and their boards of directors in connection with merger transactions, and we, our directors and Marvell may become subject to lawsuits relating to the Merger, including putative class action or derivative lawsuits, regardless of their merit. Such litigation could result in substantial costs, divert management’s attention and resources and, if a plaintiff were to obtain an injunction or other order preventing the completion of the Merger, could delay or prevent the completion of the Merger. An adverse outcome in any such litigation could also result in substantial damages or settlement costs. Litigation could also be brought in connection with any failure to complete the Merger.
